Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The narrative primarily unfolds through vivid, real-time scenes in the hospital—such as Clara eating her sandwich, talking with Ruth and Esme in the corridors, searching the nursery, and discovering the baby's sex in the bathroom. These scenes effectively build the surreal, disorienting atmosphere of the maternity ward and drive the plot toward its climax. 

At the same time, the writer skillfully weaves in brief moments of summary and exposition (such as the memory of the baby's birth, Ben's habits, Clara's copywriting job, and her feelings of unreality during pregnancy). Rather than slowing the story down, these short bursts of exposition are seamlessly integrated to provide crucial psychological context for Clara's detachment and eventual decision at the end of the story.
